issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: For a 45-year-old female auditor with combat trauma, 'Pregnancy/Birth Reminders' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items and downstream threat items center on hypervigilance, pursuit, and danger cues, whereas this item implies a reproductive/perinatal trigger theme that is not supported by the memory, threat, appraisal, or strategy content. It looks disconnected from the combat-based formulation rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: 'Restrict Eating' is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The dominant clinical pattern across triggers, threat, memory, and appraisals is fear-based hypervigilance and fragmented trauma memory, with maladaptive strategies of avoidance and rumination fitting that pattern. Restrictive eating instead suggests a separate control/body-management coping style that is not reflected elsewhere in the selected items, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same combat-related PTSD profile.

vignette:
Nadia is a 45-year-old divorced auditor, a Middle Eastern American woman who served in the Army before returning to civilian life. Three years ago, during a supply convoy in a combat zone, an IED exploded beneath the lead vehicle. She was in the back seat. The driver, a young soldier who wore a strong sandalwood cologne, and the gunner were killed instantly. Nadia survived with only a concussion, but she cannot actually recall the moment of blast. What stays with her are fragments: the dust turning the air brown, the spinning metal sound, the wet heat on her face. She has tried to piece together the seconds before impact, but there is a gap-an incomplete, broken sequence that refuses to form a whole story. When she wakes from a nightmare, the dream residue clings-the same suffocating dust, the same metallic taste-and she finds herself flooded with the absolute certainty that she should have protected them, that the event happened to her because of the sort of person she is. Her body reacts as if still in danger, heart pounding even when she is safe in her own apartment. Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning-a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been, all became potential signals of the next attack.

The smallest triggers can unravel her. A distant bang-a car backfiring, a door slamming-sends her into a spiral: she immediately begins scanning her environment, checking behind her, identifying the nearest exit. That same scanning, repeated dozens of times a day, feeds back into the fragmented quality of the memory, because she is never fully present enough to let the picture settle. The scent of a specific cologne in a department store recently sent her to the floor, and in that moment she was right back in the dust, the guilt washing over her again. She had come to believe that the gaps in her memory must mean she did something wrong-that she froze, or failed to act, and that is why she cannot remember. The more she blames herself, the more she feels she needs to watch for threats, as if the world is still out to punish her for her failure.

Her job as an auditor, which requires her to sit in a windowless office reviewing spreadsheets, has become a fragile refuge. She only feels safe in that small room, or inside her apartment. Open spaces-parking lots, the courtyard at her building-make her skin prickle with exposure. Before she can feel comfortable anywhere, she always identifies escape routes; in a grocery store, she has already mapped three ways out before she picks up a basket. When she walks down the street, she frequently looks behind her, checking if someone is following. These habits were not conscious choices; they grew slowly. At first she thought she was just being careful. But the vigilance itself reinforces the sense of threat: because she is always scanning, she is always reminded that this is a dangerous world. Living in that state of alert confirmed her deepest fear: that she really was the sort of person who brought destruction with her, and that she could not be trusted to keep others safe. And feeling that constant threat, the memory would surface without warning-the dust, the metal sound, the wet heat-as if her body was trying to stay ahead of the next explosion by reliving the last one. And the constant checking and escape planning make the memory gaps feel even larger, because she is too busy watching for future danger to let past fragments cohere.

Counterfactual thinking has become a ritual. She spends long hours imagining how life would have been different if she had stayed home that day, if she had not volunteered for the convoy, if she had insisted on a different route. The more she imagines what she could have done, the more she believes she is to blame, and the more she feels she must scan the environment for the next thing that will demand a perfect response she will not be able to give. Every time she avoids an open space-taking the long way through a corridor instead of crossing the parking lot-she confirms that the world outside is unsafe, and that she is the kind of person who cannot handle it.

She divorced two years ago. Her husband could not understand why she slept with the lights on, why she flinched at his touch if he came up behind her, why she needed to know the fire exits in every restaurant. Eventually she stopped explaining. What finally brought her to seek help was a morning last month when she woke from a nightmare, the dream residue so thick she could still smell sandalwood on her pillow, and she realized she had spent three years trying to hold together a story that would not hold. She is afraid that if she stops watching, something else will explode. But she is also afraid that if she keeps going like this, she will never feel at home in her own life again. That conviction made ordinary sounds and smells feel like warnings-a door slamming, a particular cologne, the crack of a car backfiring could all confirm that she was still at fault and still unsafe.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that the patient's negative appraisals cause external stimuli to become triggers.
The vignette does not show that a perceived threat leads to the intrusion of traumatic memories.
The vignette does not show that the sense of threat causes or reinforces negative appraisals about oneself or the world.
The vignette does not show that the perceived threat leads to increased sensitivity to triggers or makes certain stimuli become triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not show that the patient's negative appraisals cause external stimuli to become triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not show that a perceived threat leads to the intrusion of traumatic memories.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not show that the sense of threat causes or reinforces negative appraisals about oneself or the world.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not show that the perceived threat leads to increased sensitivity to triggers or makes certain stimuli become triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
